[![](data:image/png;base64,)](http://crossmark.crossref.org/dialog/?doi=10.1016/j.carbpol.2022.120102&domain=pdf)A multifunctional chitosan composite aerogel for PPCPs adsorption

Wenkun Zhang 1[, Ting Huang](#_bookmark1) 1[, Yu Ren](#_bookmark1) 1[, Shuai Yang, Xinyao Zhao, Maosen Yuan](#_bookmark1) [\*,](#_bookmark0) Jinyi Wang [\*, Qin Tu](#_bookmark0) [\*](#_bookmark0)

_College of Chemistry & Pharmacy, Northwest A&F University, Yangling, Shaanxi 712100, PR China_

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_ Chitosan aerogel Adsorption PPCPs

Antifouling Bacterial filtration Oil-water separation

A B S T R A C T

Pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) are gaining attention due to their persistence in the envi-ronment. Therefore, the development of novel adsorbents to remove them is strongly anticipated. In this study, an improved dual ice-template assembly method had been used for the preparation of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aer-ogel through ZIF-67, benzoquinone-modified graphene oxide (QGO), and sulfobetaine-modified chitosan (SB-CS) for the adsorption and removal of PPCPs in water. We reported for the first time that the chitosan composite aerogel has antifouling, bacterial filtration and oil-water separation abilities with excellent PPCPs adsorption performance and reusable, which would be a viable option for long-lasting adsorbents for PPCPs in water.

# Introduction

People have started to focus on toxins in water as their understanding of environmental preservation has grown. Pharmaceuticals and personal care products (PPCPs) have been continually polluting the aquatic environment as a result of the existing unlawful chemical discharge. The study found that there are lots of PPCPs in water, with up to 112 species ([Cheng et al., 2018](#_bookmark15); [Wang & Wang, 2016](#_bookmark45); [Wu et al., 2020](#_bookmark49)). At the same time, in-depth researches have revealed that PPCPs are easily enriched in organisms, and PPCPs in water bodies hinders the growth of algae and other plants, allowing aquatic species such as fish and mussels to reproduce, grow, and migrate at a low level ([Ebele, Abou-Elwafa](#_bookmark18) [Abdallah, & Harrad, 2017](#_bookmark18)). As a result of sewage irrigation and fertil-izers containing pollutants, PPCPs residues have been identified in edible plants, which are exceedingly detrimental to human health and the overall environment ([Chen, Gong, & Kelly, 2017](#_bookmark12)). However, the existing conventional water treatment technologies cannot effectively remove PPCPs, so it is critical to develop methods and materials for effectively removing PPCPs from water.

A variety of adsorbents are currently used to adsorb PPCPs, such as carbon materials ([Mailler et al., 2015](#_bookmark37)), clay materials ([O](#_bookmark38)¨ [zcan, Erdem, &](#_bookmark38) [O](#_bookmark38)¨ [zcan, 2005](#_bookmark38)), and nanomaterials ([Salem Attia, Hu, & Yin, 2013](#_bookmark42)). As an

excellent adsorbent, aerogel has only reported one paper on the adsorption of PPCPs so far ([Escudero-Curiel, Pazos, & Sanroma´n, 2022](#_bookmark19)), the adsorption of PPCPs in water by aerogel has not been systematically

studied. Aerogel is a nanoporous structural material, which has a high specific surface area, ultra-high porosity, adjustable open pore structure, and a chemically modifiable surface. Aerogel shows a broad application prospect in the field of water environment purification ([Wu et al., 2021](#_bookmark48)), and is expected to be utilized for PPCPs adsorption in water. Meanwhile, because there are a large number of pathogens in unsafe water, biofouling has been considered as a difficult problem for aerogel adsorbent ([Wu et al., 2021](#_bookmark48)). Let's imagine that if the aerogel can effec-tively adsorb PPCPs while giving it the antifouling, this problem will be resolved.

Graphene oxide (GO) has a large number of oxygen-containing functional groups to more effectively adsorb PPCPs in water ([Lou](#_bookmark34) [et al., 2020](#_bookmark34)). Also, GO has been shown to inactivate pathogens and limit microbial adhesion ([Cao et al., 2022](#_bookmark11); [Zhang et al., 2017](#_bookmark53)). However, the poor stability of GO-based aerogel in water caused by strong interaction with H2O will cause secondary pollution ([Qin, Deng, Huang, & Tong,](#_bookmark40) [2022](#_bookmark40)). So it must modify GO to create composite aerogel. Chitosan (CS) is a natural polysaccharide, which not only performs great adsorption but also has strong antibacterial property ([Madni, Kousar, Naeem, &](#_bookmark36) [Wahid, 2021](#_bookmark36)). More importantly, it can maintain the characteristics of GO monolayer, ensuring that the material structure can be regulated and functionalized ([Li et al., 2016](#_bookmark26); [Liu et al., 2018](#_bookmark33); [Sahnoun & Boutahala,](#_bookmark41) [2018](#_bookmark41); [Vunain, Mishra, & Mamba, 2016](#_bookmark43)). Discovered by the latest research of chitosan, a new green method can be used for the extraction and processing of chitosan. This is the reason why chitosan has good

commercial value ([Huq, Khan, Brown, Dhaya, & He, 2022](#_bookmark23)). Therefore, we want to synthesize a composite aerogel composed of GO and CS (GO/ CS) to adsorb PPCPs in water with antifouling. To enhance the anti-fouling of GO/CS aerogel, we used benzoquinone to modify GO (QGO), which has been reported with a strong antibacterial ability ([Guo, Dun-das, Zhou, Johnston, & Yu, 2021](#_bookmark22)). Meanwhile, we introduced zwitter-ionic sulfobetaine with antifouling property onto CS (SB-CS) ([Dong](#_bookmark17) [et al., 2016](#_bookmark17)). Furthermore, because the materials of synthetic aerogel are hydrophilic, the prepared aerogel may be used for oil-water separation. Thus far, the chitosan aerogel for PPCPs adsorption with antifouling, bacterial filtration, and oil-water separation properties have not yet been reported.

In addition, we designed the following methods to enhance the adsorption capacity of the aerogel. Firstly, ZIF-67 is a special kind of MOFs porous material. Because of its stable coordination bonds, it is

easy to introduce ligand functional groups, so that ZIF-67 can adsorb PPCPs through electrostatic attraction, π-π interaction and hydrogen bonding ([Ighalo et al., 2022](#_bookmark24); [Li, Guo, Zhu, & Yan, 2019](#_bookmark27)). However, if

ZIF-67 is used alone as adsorbent, its recovery ability is very poor ([Luo](#_bookmark35) [et al., 2020](#_bookmark35); [Yang et al., 2018](#_bookmark51)), QGO/SB-CS aerogel is a good carrier to support ZIF-67. ZIF-67 can be created _in situ_ inside the aerogel. Sec-ondly, at present, there are numerous methods for the preparation of aerogels, such as ordinary vacuum freeze-drying and supercritical dry-ing ([Cheng et al., 2017](#_bookmark14); [Ganesamoorthy, Vadivel, Kumar, Kushwaha, &](#_bookmark20) [Mamane, 2021](#_bookmark20)). Recently, it has been reported that the preparation of nanocellulose aerogel by the dual ice-template method (DITA) has greatly changed its adsorption ability ([Qin et al., 2021](#_bookmark39); [Wang, Liu,](#_bookmark44) [Wang, & Li, 2018](#_bookmark44)). Guided by the idea, in this study, we prepared ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel by the improved DITA to enhance its mechani-cal property and adsorption capacity. The specific DITA method is as

follows: (1) we frozen SB-CS in —196 ◦C liquid nitrogen to construct a

sub-micron fibrous structure; (2) After cross-linking through amide bonds to form the sol-gel system of SB-CS and QGO, we again frozen the solution through —196 ◦C liquid nitrogen, and then vacuum-freeze-dried

for 48 h to prepare QGO/SB-CS aerogel.

Built on the above analysis, we hypothesize that the combination of ZIF-67, QGO, and SB-CS will obtain a multifunctional composite aero-gel. Through an improved DITA method, we will prepare ZIF-67/QGO/ SB-CS aerogel with special pore structure, which will beneficial for absorbing PPCPs. Therefore, we will study the mechanical property, stability, antifouling, bacteria filtration, oil-water separation and the adsorption capacity for PPCPs of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel. In addi-tion, the adsorption kinetics and isotherms of TC on aerogel, and the reusability of the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel will be also investigated.

# Materials and methods

- 1.  _Materials_

Graphene oxide (GO) was purchased from XFNANO, Inc. (Nanjing, China). Chitosan of high viscosity (>400 mPa.s, ≥95 % deacetylated) was purchased from Aladdin (Shanghai, China). Benzoquinone was

obtained from Tianjin Kermel (Tianjin, China). Ethanol absolute, Cobaltous nitrate hexahydrate \[Co(NO3)2⋅6H2O\], and agar powder were purchased from Beijing Chemical Works (Beijing, China). 1-chloro-3-dimethylaminopropane hydrochloride (CDMAP⋅HCl), 1,3-propane sul-fonic acid, 1,2-dichloroethane, Trimesic acid (H3BTC), Doxorubicin

hydrochloride (DOX), Tetracycline (TC), Cobalt sulfate (CoSO4), Rifampicin (RFP), Ibuprofen (IBP), and Metronidazole (MNZ) were purchased from Aladdin Reagent (Shanghai, China). The _Escherichia coli_ HB101 (_E. coli_) and _Staphylococcus aureus_ (_S. aureus_) live cultures were supplied by Prof. Peng Chen of Northwest A & F University (Yangling, China). Yeast extract and tryptone were obtained from Oxoid Ltd. (Basingstoke, Hampshire, England).

- 1.  _Fabrication of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel_

The synthesis of Sulfobetaine Chitosan (SB-CS), Benzoquinone-modified Graphene Oxide (QGO), and Characterization were placed in the Supporting Information. First, QGO (10 mg/L) was dispersed in distilled water (1 mL) using ultrasound. SB-CS (15 mg/L) was dissolved in 0.1 M acetic acid solution (1 mL), added to the above QGO suspen-sion, and vigorously stirred until a stable suspension was formed. After freezing the suspension with liquid nitrogen, it was lyophilized by

vacuum for 48 h. Then, Co(NO3)2⋅6H2O (0.733 g) was added to react for

12 h, then 2-methylimidazole (1.623 g) was added to react for another 12 h, and the solution was dried by vacuum to obtain the ZIF-67/QGO/ SB-CS aerogel ([Li et al., 2020](#_bookmark25); [Liang et al., 2019](#_bookmark29)).

- 1.  _Bacterial filtration and antibacterial experiments of aerogel_

The bacterial filtration and antibacterial experiments of aerogel was evaluated according to a previous publication ([Wang et al., 2021](#_bookmark47); [Zhang](#_bookmark55) [et al., 2020](#_bookmark55)). The Supporting Information shows the detailed procedures.

- 1.  _Oil-water separation experiment of aerogel_

Oil-water separation tests of aerogel was evaluated according to a previous publication ([Lin, Yang, Jeong, Chang, & Hong, 2016](#_bookmark31); [Zhang](#_bookmark56) [et al., 2019](#_bookmark56); [Zhang et al., 2019](#_bookmark54)). The Supporting Information shows the detailed procedures.

- 1.  _Adsorption measurements_

The adsorption capacity of aerogel for PPCPs was evaluated ac-cording to a previous publication ([Wang et al., 2019](#_bookmark46)). The Supporting Information shows the detailed procedures.

- 1.  _Reusability_

The regeneration of used adsorbents is critical for economic. The reusability of the aerogel was evaluated according to a previous publi-cation ([Conde-Cid et al., 2019](#_bookmark16)). The Supporting Information shows the detailed procedures.

# Results and discussion

- 1.  _Synthesis of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel_

The ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel fabricating process was illustrated in [Scheme 1](#_bookmark2). Firstly, zwitterionic sulfobetaine-modified chitosan (SB-CS) was synthesized. SB-CS can be built into numerous morphologies (such as fibers, ribbons, and films) _via_ ice-templating processes due to the abundance of surface amino and hydroxyl groups. Because of the suppression of the creation of massive ice crystals, such constructed morphology may be easily regulated by varied freezing temperatures, generating a sub-micron fiber morphology when subjected to an

extremely low temperature (such as utilizing liquid nitrogen at —196 ◦C) ([Qin et al., 2021](#_bookmark39)). So we froze SB-CS in —196 ◦C liquid nitrogen to

construct a sub-micron fibrous structure. Secondly, after cross-linking through amide bonds to form the sol-gel system of SB-CS and benzoquinone-modified graphene oxide (QGO), we again frozen the solution through —196 ◦C liquid nitrogen, and then vacuum-freeze-dried for 48 h to get QGO/SB-CS aerogel. Because for the traditional method of

preparing aerogel, aerogel can be fabricated by directly freezing its aqueous suspension at —17 ◦C, obtaining a honeycomb-like structure with a few hundred micrometers of huge holes as a result of the for-

mation of massive ice crystals at a relatively high temperature under low freezing rate. Contrarily, when exposed to an extremely low tempera-ture (such as using liquid nitrogen at —196 ◦C) due to the inhibition of

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Scheme 1.** Illustration of the preparation process of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel and its properties.

the growth of large ice crystals, aerogel can be yielding a honeycomb-like structure with a micrometers of small pores ([Qin et al., 2021](#_bookmark39)). Finally, QGO/SB-CS aerogel was immersed in the solution of Co (NO3)2⋅6H2O and 2-methylimidazole to generate ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel _in situ_.

Motivated by the significantly varied constructed morphologies influenced by changing the freezing conditions, the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was developed following two steps, including (I) assembling SB-

CS at —196 ◦C into continuous sub-micron fibrous structure; and (II) after a freezing treatment at —196 ◦C, vacuum freeze-drying was used to

produce aerogels with small pore sizes. Such a strategy was referred to as improving dual ice-templating assembly (DITA). To prove the superi-ority of the aerogel prepared by DITA, another three aerogels were prepared by different methods as controls: GO/CS aerogel (without I&II), QGO/SB-CS aerogel (without II) and ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel (without I).

- 1.  _Microstructure of aerogel_

ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was ultra-light, as illustrated in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark3)a-d, and could be placed on relatively light substrates (such as weighing paper, dried flowers, and dried wheat) without deforming them. We observed the internal micro-structure of the aerogel by SEM. As can be seen from the [Fig. 1](#_bookmark3)e-h, GO/CS aerogel (without I&II), which be pre-

pared by vacuum freeze-drying at —17 ◦C directly, because of the for-

mation of large ice crystals, it had a larger honeycomb-like hole structure. For QGO/SB-CS aerogel (without II), after the first step of

liquid nitrogen freezing (—196 ◦C), then obtained by vacuum freeze-drying at —17 ◦C, formed a large honeycomb-like pore structure, and a sub-micron structure. Afterwards, ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel

(without I) without DITA showed no sub-micron fibrous morphology, forming a smaller honeycomb-like pore structure, which was due to that the SB-CS was not treated with liquid nitrogen (—196 ◦C), but the sol-gel

system was treated with liquid nitrogen (—196 ◦C), causing it to form

smaller ice crystals. Finally, as showed in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark3)h, ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel with DITA had a smaller honeycomb-like pore structure. In addition, it also existed sub-micron fiber morphology.

In order to observe its pore structure more clearly, we obtained the cross-sectional SEM images of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel with DITA under different magnifications, as showed in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark3)i-l. These images showed ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel with DITA contained the honeycomb-like as well as spider web-like pores, and the pore structure and size were both uniform. The inset image of [Fig. 1](#_bookmark3)l was the crystal structure of ZIF-67 in the aerogel. It can be found that there was a large amount of ZIF-67. These results demonstrated the excellent porosity of the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel prepared by DITA. Porous architecture offered an abundance of active location for PPCPs molecules to penetrate.

In addition, [Fig. 2](#_bookmark4)a-d showed the SEM images of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogels (DITA) prepared with different mass fractions of SB-CS (20 %, 40 %, 60 %, 80 %). With the increase of SB-CS, the cross-linking of QGO and SB-CS was more sufficient, resulting in smaller pore size ([Fig. 2](#_bookmark4)e-h). When the mass fraction of SB-CS was 60 %, the pore size distribution of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was the most uniform and the porosity was

the largest (about 55 %, [Fig. 2](#_bookmark4)i). During the experimental exploration stage, it was found that when the mass fraction of SB-CS was <20 % and

\>80 %, the aerogel cannot be obtained. Therefore, we added the SB-CS

with mass fraction of 60 % to synthesize ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel in the study. The porous nature of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS was measured by nitrogen gas physisorption measurements (Fig. S2). The sorption-desorption isotherms exhibited a typical IV hysteresis loop. Calcula-tion using the sorption data resulted in a surface area of 18.536 m2/g for the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel. In addition, a vertical rapid increase at the relative pressure of approximately 1.0 demonstrated the macro-porosity of the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel. At the same time, open macropores were observed in SEM images. By calculation, the density of the aerogel was 0.01 g/cm3.

Aerogel with good water absorption can offer a strong foundation for eliminating water contaminants. The compressed ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel may return to its original shape in the water in 30 s, as seen in Fig. S3a-b and Video S1, which exhibited the excellent water absorption ability of the aerogel. Meanwhile, the Video S1 and Fig. S3c-d confirmed that the synthesized ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel had excellent water stability, the QGO and ZIF-67 would not leak from the aerogel, and the structure of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel remained intact after 24 h of immersion in water.

- 1.  _Characterization of aerogel_

XRD, FT-IR, and XPS were utilized to confirm the chemical compo-sition of the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel. The typical peaks of synthe-sized ZIF-67 emerged at 2θ = 7.39◦, 10.36◦, 12.79◦, 14.71◦, 16.45◦,

18.01◦, 22.19◦, 24.64◦, 26.72◦ ([Yang et al., 2018](#_bookmark51)), as shown in the XRD

patterns ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark5)a), which was comparable with the characteristic peaks of the simulated ZIF-67. In the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS spectrum, there were recognizable ZIF-67 peaks, showing that ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel contained a full ZIF-67 crystal structure. Compared XRD curves of CS, QGO/SB-CS, and ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, all the characteristic peak of QGO and CS appeared in the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS spectrum. However, due to the influence of QGO and SB-CS during synthesis, its

characteristic peak intensity of QGO and SB-CS in the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS was weakened.

In order to further examine the composition of the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, we performed FT-IR analysis on it ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark5)b-c). The C–O peak at 1719 cm—1, the graphitic C–C peak at 1630 cm—1, the deformation vibration of O–H peak at 1370 cm—1, the stretching vibration of alkoxy group peak at 1220 cm—1, the stretching vibration of epoxy group peak at 1050 cm—1 were the characteristic peaks for pure GO ([Mailler et al.,](#_bookmark37) [2015](#_bookmark37); [Zhang et al., 2021](#_bookmark57)). In the FT-IR spectrum of QGO, a relatively

strong peak appeared at 1656 cm—1 (C=O), which was due to the addition of benzoquinone. Pure CS showed characteristic peaks at 1566

cm—1 (N–H), 1413 cm—1 (C–N), 1078 cm—1 (C–O). In the spectrum of SB-CS, 1650 cm—1 (C=O) and 1554 cm—1 (N–H) were the characteristic peaks of two amide bonds, the peaks at 1470 cm—1 (N–C) and 1201 cm—1 (S–O) were attributed to nitrogen-containing groups and sulfonic

acid groups in zwitterionic SB. As showed in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark5)c, in the FT-IR of GO/

CS, in addition to the characteristic peaks of GO and CS, amide I

appeared at 1650 cm—1 (C=O) and amide II bands appeared at 1548 cm—1 (N–H) in GO/CS, indicating that GO was successfully cross-linked with CS through -NH-C=O-. QGO/SB-CS aerogel had similar charac-teristic peaks at 1650 cm—1 (C=O) and 1548 cm—1 (N–H). Two new characteristic peaks at 992 cm—1 (C–N) and 422 cm—1 (Co–N)

appeared in the spectrum of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, which was ascribed to the characteristics peak of the ZIF-67(Q. [Yang et al., 2018](#_bookmark51)). In the XPS wide scan data for GO/CS, QGO/SB-CS, and ZIF-67/QGO/

SB-CS aerogel ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark5)d), Peaks for carbon (C 1s at 284.5 eV), nitrogen (N 1s at 400.0 eV), and oxygen (O 1s at 531.0 eV) were visible in all aer-ogels ([Zhang, Ma, et al., 2019](#_bookmark54); [Zhang, Wang, et al., 2019](#_bookmark56)). The aerogels ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS and QGO/SB-CS included the S2p signal. The ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel's XPS broad scan spectrum revealed new Co2p signal peaks. This demonstrated that the Co element was present. Further evidence of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was achieved by high-resolution S2p and Co2p XPS spectra. High-resolution XPS spectrum of

S2p of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS, in which the peak at 166.5 eV is assigned to sulfobetaine sulfonate anion (-SO—) ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark5)e). In the high-resolution spectrum of Co2p ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark5)f), two major peaks at 796.4 and 781.3 eV

were the characteristics of Co2p1/2 and Co2p3/2, respectively. And the Co2p3/2 was characteristic of Co2+ species, which was characteristic peak for the ZIF-67. The above data fully demonstrated the successful

preparation of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel.

The thermal stability of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was evaluated using TGA analysis. As showed in [Fig. 3](#_bookmark5)g, the TGA curves were obtained

by immersing the aerogels in a N2 stream at a temperature of 26–800 ◦C. Throughout the process, QGO lost a small amount of weight, resulting in a final weight loss of about 64 %. For SB-CS, between 0 and 200 ◦C, the mass loss was 17.7 % due to the decomposition of SB and part of the water. When >200 ◦C, the chitosan began to decompose by itself, the weight loss was about 79.4 %. For ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, the first weight loss was noticed in the temperature range of 50 to 100 ◦C due to

the volatilization of the water adsorbed on the surface, and the weight loss was about 10.2 %. The ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel lost 20 % of its mass as the temperature rose from 100 to 200 ◦C due to the dissolution

of the oxygen-containing functional groups of QGO and the decompo-

sition of SB. Weight loss in the 250–500 ◦C range was related to the breakdown of unstable nitrogen- and oxygen-containing groups in SB-CS, with a mass loss of approximately 85.2 %. The sudden mass loss

above 500 ◦C was attributed to the decomposition of the organic ligands of ZIF-67 and chitosan, resulting in a final residual mass of 10.8 %.

Meanwhile, we investigated the mechanical properties of ZIF-67/ QGO/SB-CS aerogel. From the stress-strain curves of the aerogels ([Fig. 3](#_bookmark5)h), it can be observed that the synthesized aerogels have excellent flexibility and robustness. The ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel's compres-sive stress gradually increased as the amount of chitosan in the material increased. This established chitosan's ability to enhance the mechanical qualities of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogels. Comparing the GO/CS aerogel with the QGO/SB-CS aerogel, it was found that the compressive resis-tance of the GO/CS aerogel was not as good as that of the QGO/SB-CS aerogel. It was because during the synthesis of SB-CS, the sub-micron structure was formed by freezing treatment with liquid nitrogen, which made the compression resistance of QGO/SB-CS aerogels greater than that of GO/CS aerogel. Freezing treatment with liquid nitrogen was the key step in the dual ice-template method. The effect of the dual ice-template method on the mechanical properties of aerogel was demon-strated. It can be found that ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS (when the SB-CS con-tent is 80 %, 0.1 g in mass, 1 cm in high, and 1 cm2 in surface area) had a maximum compressive capacity of 2.5 MPa when the deformation reached 80 %. It can be concluded that the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel prepared by improved DITA exhibited excellent mechanical property. In addition, it could be seen from Fig. S4 that the structure did not collapse after the aerogel was compressed.

- 1.  _Antifouling and bacterial filtration properties of aerogel_

In order to study the antibacterial activity of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, we used _E. coli_ as the model bacteria to analysis by the clas-sical plate counting method, and set the blank and GO/CS aerogel as the control groups. The result ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)b) showed GO/CS and ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogels had good antibacterial activity, while the antibacterial ability of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was preferable to that of GO/CS aerogel. In order to investigate ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel's antibacte-rial properties further, the absorbance at 600 nm (OD600) of the cell suspension was evaluated after the _E. coli_ and _S. aureus_ co-culturing with these aerogels for 2, 4, and 6 h ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)d and e). The _E. coli_ reduction after co-culturing with the GO/CS aerogel was 7.8 % (2 h), 40.1 % (4 h), and

61.1 % (6 h), respectively. The _E. coli_ reduction of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was 10.1 %, 47.5 %, and 88.6 %, respectively. The same experiment was further performed on _S. aureus_. The _S. aureus_ reduction after co-culturing with the GO/CS aerogel was 10.1 % (2 h), 39.5 % (4 h) and 65.5 % (6 h), respectively. The _S. aureus_ reduction of ZIF-67/QGO/ SB-CS aerogel was 18.3 %, 59.5 % and 87.5 %, respectively. This meant that GO/CS and ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel had good antibacterial ef-fects on both _E. coli_ and _S. aureus_, and the antibacterial efficiency increased with time. Compared to the GO/CS with ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, the antibacterial efficiency of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was significantly higher than that of GO/CS aerogel. It was attributed to the effect of benzoquinone and SB. Because the quinone group has an antibacterial effect, and SB has antibacterial properties due to the presence of the strongly sulfonic acid functional group, which makes ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel has more excellent antibacterial property.

Finally, we investigated the bacterial filtration ability of ZIF-67/ QGO/SB-CS aerogel by measuring the OD600 of the cell suspension before and after filtered by ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel. The ZIF-67/ QGO/SB-CS aerogel was loaded in a syringe volume and bacterial cul-ture (_E. coli_ and _S. aureus_) was filtered through it. [Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)a showed images of bacterial culture before and after filtered by the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel. The color of the bacterial culture solution became lighter after filtered by ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, which proved that the aerogel had a certain ability to remove _E. coli_ and _S. aureus_. [Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)c summarized the reduction of _E. coli_ and _S. aureus_ bacteria for the ZIF-67/ QGO/SB-CS aerogel in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)a. The filtration removal efficiency of the aerogel arrived at 72.5 % for _E. coli_ and 49.0 % for _S. aureus_, the dif-ference in removal efficiency may be caused by the higher initial

- 1.  _Oil-water separation_

To evaluate the applicability of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel in oil-water separation, the gravity-driven separation was achieved using an apparatus made of a funnel and a glass bottle. As showed in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)a-c, the mixture was poured into the top funnel, and since the aerogel was hy-drophilic and had holes that allowed water to pass through, the water phase permeated the aerogel and accumulated at the bottom of the glass container ([Yue et al., 2022](#_bookmark52)). Aerogel's water-thin coating that formed on it may stop oil entering the pores. So the oil was retained above the prepared aerogel. With the oil/water combination for six cycles, the recyclability was studied. ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)d-f). It was found the separation effi-ciencies of oil/water (vegetable oil, silicone oil, engine oil) could still be maintained above 90 % after 6 cycles. The fluxes of vegetable oil, sili-cone oil, engine oil-water were 579, 1737, 3474 L/m2 h, respectively ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)g). Variable flux for various oil-water combinations may suggest that variations in pressure on the aerogel are caused by variations in oil viscosity. Video S2 showed the oil-water separation experiment. All the results demonstrated that the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel had outstanding oil-water separation ability. Furthermore, the ZIF-67/QGO/ SB-CS aerogel is a good option for use in practical oil-water separation because of its exceptional recyclability and high efficiency.

- 1.  _Adsorption of TC_

Next, we studied the adsorption performance of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel to tetracycline (TC), which is the most common and represen-tative pollutant in PPCPs. As shown in Fig. S5, the UV–vis spectra of TC

solution after being exposed to 4 different aerogels (GO/CS, QGO/SB-

CS, ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS without DITA, ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS with DITA),

as time passed, it was evident that the absorbance of the TC solution had greatly decreased. After 180 min, the absorbance of TC almost remained unchanged, so it could be considered that the adsorption reached satu-ration after 180 min. We constructed the standard curve between the concentration of TC and the absorbance of TC to more clearly illustrate

the adsorption of TC by aerogel. Fig. S6 demonstrated that the standard curve's correlation coefficient (R2) was 0.9998, which could accurately depict the connection between absorbance and concentration. We selected the initial concentration of TC solution to be 100 mg/L for adsorption, the adsorption capacity of different aerogels for TC was illustrated in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark8)a. As can be viewed, the addition of ZIF-67 improved the adsorption capacity of aerogel, because there were electrostatic

attraction and π-π interaction between TC and ZIF-67, and a hydrogen

bond may be formed between them. ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel pre-pared by DITA had much greater adsorption capacity for TC than the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel (without DITA) prepared by the common method. Better adsorption capacity of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel with DITA was due to the honeycomb-like as well as spider web-like pores, and the uniform pore structure, which were beneficial for generating more active sites.

After that, we studied the effect of different initial concentrations of TC solutions (50–600 mg/L) on the adsorption capacity of aerogels, as shown in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark8)b, when the initial concentration of TC was 50–400 mg/L, _qe_ increased rapidly because the adsorbed TC in the aerogels occupies

the active sites on the aerogels. When the TC concentration over 400 mg/L, the adsorption of TC on the aerogels was close to saturation and thus tended to be stable. The adsorption capacity of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel to TC also increased with an increase in SB-CS content when the mass of QGO remained constant. This was due to the amino group of SB-CS being advantageous to the adsorption of TC. When the mass fraction of SB-CS was 60 %, the most uniform pore size distribution and the most number of pores were favorable for _in situ_ growth of ZIF-67 on the aerogel, thereby enhancing the adsorption capacity of TC on the ZIF-67/ QGO/SB-CS aerogel. As a result, we hypothesized that the TC adsorption on the aerogel was a combination of chemical adsorption (surface functional groups) and physical adsorption (pore size and pore number). When QGO was 10 mg/mL and the mass fraction of SB-CS was 60 %, the adsorption capacity of aerogel for TC was as high as 1375 mg/g due to the combined impact of chemisorption and physical adsorption. To further demonstrate the adsorption process, we used a ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel produced by DITA with a QGO concentration of 10 mg/mL and an SB-CS mass fraction of 60 % to analyze adsorption isotherms and

- 1.  _Adsorption isotherm_

Four widely used isotherms, including Langmuir, Freundlich, Sips, and Temkin, have been employed to characterize solid-liquid adsorption systems (The isotherm parameters and equations of Sips and Temkin

models were given in Table S1) ([Zhang et al., 2021](#_bookmark57)).

[Fig. 6](#_bookmark8)c-f were the fitting curve of the adsorption isothermal model of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel. The correlation coefficient (R2) of the Freundlich model, Langmuir model, Sips model and Temkin model was 0.9663, 0.9992, 0.9688, and 0.8064, respectively. The ZIF-67/QGO/SB-

CS aerogel isotherm data could be observed to be best described by the Langmuir model, with an _R2_ value of >0.9990, indicating that the

**Fig. 7.** (a) Variation of adsorption amount (_qt_, mg/g) of TC with increasing adsorption time (_t_, h) by the ZIF-67/QGO-SB-CS aerogel; (b-d) corresponding simulation plots obtained through the pseudo-first-order model, pseudo-second-order adsorption model, and Weber-Morris adsorption kinetic model, respectively.

adsorption of TC by the aerogel was a single layer adsorption. Table S2 listed the fitting parameters of the Langmuir and Freundlich models. The Freundlich model n (2.4691) was used to evaluate the adsorption ability. The values of n between 2 and 10 suggested a high adsorption capacity, which also mirrored the greater adsorption capacity of the synthesized ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel. The Langmuir model obtained a separation factor (RL) of 0.065, suggesting that the adsorption process was favor-able. The fitting parameters of the Sips and Temkin models were pro-vided in Table S3.

- 1.  _Adsorption kinetics_

Adsorption rate is an important measure for evaluating adsorbent performance and understanding the adsorption process. At the initial TC concentration (400 mg/L), as shown in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark9)a. In stage I, TC adsorption capacity was as high as 1200 mg/g in <50 min. Due to the total utili-zation of the available active surface sites, it progressively acquired a

saturation adsorption capacity of 1375 mg/g in stage II ([Zhang et al.,](#_bookmark57) [2021](#_bookmark57)).

Pseudo-first order and pseudo-second-order models were used to better examine the adsorption process including mass transfer and chemical reaction. According to the fitting curves for the pseudo-first-order model ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark9)b) and the pseudo-second-order model ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark9)c), the correlation coefficient for the pseudo-second-order model was sub-

stantially higher (R2 = 0.9982) than for the pseudo-first-order model (R2 = 0.7452). The estimated qe using the pseudo-second-order model (qe, cal = 1500 mg/g) was substantially closer to the experimental qe (qe, expl = 1375 mg/g) for the fitted values reported in Table S4. As a consequence, the experimental data fit well for the pseudo-second-order

model, indicating a rate-limiting phase mediated by chemical reaction as a result of valence force interaction _via_ exchanging electrons between TC molecules and adsorbent surface. For the intraparticle diffusion model ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark9)d), the plots of _qt vs. t0.5_ contained two portions of straight lines, showing that the TC adsorption process by the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was a two-step process that included external surface adsorption and progressive adsorption. Because of the high concentration of TC in the solution and the existence of a significant number of adsorption sites on the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, the results revealed that TC adsorption by the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was highly rapid in the first stage. Aside from the effect of intraparticle diffusion, boundary layer diffusion influenced TC adsorption in this procedure. The intra-particle diffusion rate was considerably reduced in the later stage due to the simultaneous lowering of the TC concentration and the adsorption sites ([Zhang et al., 2021](#_bookmark57)).

Table S5 compared the maximal adsorption capacity of TC to that of other reported adsorbents. The adsorption capacity of the ZIF-67/QGO/ SB-CS aerogel was good (1375 mg/g). It is possible to infer that the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel is not only more effective than usual adsorbents, but also similar to other reported GO ([Xia et al., 2022](#_bookmark50)) aerogel and ZIF-

67 ([Liu, Xu, & Li, 2021](#_bookmark32)) in the literature. In contrast to others that rely more on physical modification, the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel adsor-bent is primarily mediated by the synergistic impact of physical modi-fication and chemical reaction. ([Chen et al., 2021](#_bookmark13)).

- 1.  _Adsorption of PPCPs and reuse of aerogel_

In order to prove that ZIF/QGO/SB-CS aerogel has adsorption ca-pacity for different PPCPs, we selected six representative pollutants

{Doxorubicin hydrochloride (DOX, the initial concentration is 10 mg/L), Tetracycline (TC, the initial concentration is 400 mg/L), Cobalt sulfate (CoSO4, the initial concentration is 1300 mg/L), Rifampicin (RFP, the initial concentration is 1000 mg/L), Ibuprofen (IBP, the initial concen-tration is 10 mg/L), and Metronidazole (MNZ, the initial concentration is 100 mg/L)} for independent adsorption studies. It could be observed from [Fig. 8](#_bookmark10)a that ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel also had excellent adsorption performance for different PPCPs. The adsorption capacity of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel for six PPCPs could reach 1300 mg/g (DOX), 1375 mg/g (TC), 1100 mg/g (CoSO4), 100 mg/g (RFP), 250 mg/

g (IBP) and 300 mg/g (MNZ), respectively. Compared with another four PPCPs, the adsorption capacity of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was relatively low to IBP and MNZ, but for the adsorbents that have been developed and reported so far for IBP ([Liao et al., 2018](#_bookmark30)) and MNZ ([Ghiasi, Solaimany Nazar, Farhadian, Tangestaninejad, & Emami,](#_bookmark21) [2022](#_bookmark21)), the adsorption capacity of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel is also good.

From an industrial standpoint, the capacity of adsorbents to regen-erate is a critical component in determining cost-effectiveness. To evaluate the regeneration ability of the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, the treatment of washing with 0.01 M CaCl2 aqueous solution was per-formed to recover the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel after adsorbing TC. [Fig. 8](#_bookmark10)b showed the result of six recyclability studies of the ZIF-67/QGO/ SB-CS aerogel for TC. After 2 cycles, the adsorption capacity of the aerogel to TC was almost unchanged (1375 mg/g _vs_ 1300 mg/g). It was worthy of note that the adsorption capacity of the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel could still reach 50 % of the first use after 6 cycles, indicating superior cycling stability of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel. The decrease in adsorption capacity of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel may be explained by the damage of its surface structure. The remarkable reusability exhibited by the aerogel indicated that the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel can be used as a cost-effective PPCPs adsorbent for practical wastewater treatment ([Li & Shi, 2022](#_bookmark28)).

# Conclusions

In summary, a highly functional composite aerogel were obtained by ZIF-67, QGO, and SB-CS using the improved dual ice-template method. The aerogel that not only had great mechanical strength and low den-sity, but also possessed antifouling, bacterial filtration, and oil-water

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 8.** (a) The adsorption capacity of ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel towards different types of PPCPs; (b) The absorption recyclability of the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel for TC.

separation properties. Meanwhile, ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel had excellent adsorption performance for novel pollutants PPCPs {(DOX, 1300 mg/g), (TC, 1375 mg/g), (CoSO4, 1100 mg/g), (RFP, 100 mg/g), (IBP, 250 mg/g) and (MNZ, 300 mg/g)}. Using tetracycline as a typical PPCPs pollutant to verify the adsorption mechanism of aerogel to PPCPs, the results confirmed that the adsorption isotherm of tetracycline on ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel was more in accordance with the Langmuir isotherm model, indicating that the adsorption was a monolayer adsorption. According to the pseudo-second-order kinetic equation for tetracycline adsorption on the ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel, chemical adsorption was the primary adsorption mechanism. Furthermore, the prepared ZIF-67/QGO/SB-CS aerogel exhibited only a small activity loss after six-cycle consecutive usage. All the results confirm that ZIF-67/ QGO/SB-CS aerogel can be used as an adsorbent for PPCPs with anti-fouling, bacterial filtration, and oil-water separation properties and has great potential in purification application of wastewater.
